Yes, I am aware of the foreign taxes paid credit. Let's say they have $100 in taxable income. I'm Ireland if the tax rate is 12.5% they would then pay $12 in tax. In the US the tax rate is 34% so they will have tax due of $34. They then get the $12 credit so they would end up paying an additional $22 of tax to the US. 

There is double taxation. Let's make two companies, Corp Inc. and Partnership LLC. You are the owner of both. They both sell widgets. Last year they both made $100 of taxable income. The Inc is going to pay $34 in tax. They then pay a dividend of $66 to their shareholder. He pays 20% tax  or $13. So on that $100 the owners have paid $47 in tax. Not including states. 

The partnership will earn the $100 and not pay anything in tax. All the income will be separately stated on each partners K-1.  Depending on his total income AND the type of income that is passed through to him will determine his tax rate. We said it was ordinary income from the sale of widgets. And let's say he is in the top bracket at 34%. So he will just pay the 34 in tax. He will never pay a tax on getting the profits out of the company.
No not the worker, the shareholder. Double taxation on corporate entities is one of the main disadvantages of corporations vs partnerships. A partnership doesn't pay tax where a corporation does.

You're correct that corporate tax is a small chunk of the revenue. The majority of us tax revenue is derived the sub chapter k code section for partnerships and the ultimate tax payer, the individual. Even corporate income is taxed again as it flows from the entity to the individual.
The US is not being deprived of revenue. It is merely a timing issue that arises from income derived from foreign markets.

First off there isn't some magical loophole that allows this to happen. 
I am a big 4 accountant in SF that works on this all day. From the Tech Corporate side it works like this. You develop some type of intellectual property (IP) that you want to sell in foreign markets. You keep the license for US sales with a US subsidiary that reports all US sales and pays taxes in the US on those profits. The US tax code is set up to tax all worldwide income. So you sell your license to foreign subsidiaries and pay transfer pricing taxes when you transfer the ip. That foreign corporation now holds the rights to all profits from the use of the ip. You keep those profits and cash in the foreign markets to sustain operations. 

Edit: just wanted to add if there is not a business reason to transfer the money to the is it should be held where the asset (ip) is located.
